paragraphs.heading: What primates are
paragraphs.text: Primates are an order of mammals split into two groups. The strepsirrhines include lemurs, galagos and lorisids; the haplorhines include tarsiers and the simians, meaning monkeys and apes. Depending on the classification used, there are 376–524 living species, and new ones keep being found: over 25 were described in the 2000s and 36 in the 2010s. They range from Madame Berthe's mouse lemur, at 30 g, to the eastern gorilla, at over 200 kg.

paragraphs.heading: Big brains, sharp eyes
paragraphs.text: For their body size, primates have large brains compared with other mammals. They depend more on sharp eyesight and less on smell, which is the leading sense in most mammals. These traits are strongest in monkeys and apes and noticeably weaker in lorises and lemurs. Primates also develop more slowly than other mammals of similar size, reach maturity later and live longer.

paragraphs.heading: Trees and ground
paragraphs.text: Every primate species has adaptations for climbing trees, though some, such as gorillas, humans and baboons, live mainly on the ground. In the trees, primates leap from one tree to the next or swing between branches, which is called brachiation. On the ground they may walk on two hindlimbs, called bipedalism, or on all four limbs by knuckle-walking.

paragraphs.heading: Social and clever
paragraphs.text: Primates are among the most social of all animals, living as pairs or family groups, harems with a single male, or groups with several males and several females. They are also the most cognitively advanced animals. Humans create complex languages and civilizations, and other primates have been recorded using tools. Primates may communicate with facial and hand gestures, smells and vocal sounds.

paragraphs.heading: Names that do not fit
paragraphs.text: The word primates comes, through French, from Latin meaning "first" or "chief", and Carl Linnaeus gave the name because he thought this the "highest" order of animals. Familiar group names such as prosimians, monkeys and great apes come from an older method of arranging living primates in a series leading up to humans. Several of these groups are paraphyletic, meaning they leave out some descendants of a common ancestor. "Monkeys", for example, leaves out the hominoids, the group of apes and humans, even though they descend from the same ancestor.

paragraphs.heading: Under threat
paragraphs.text: About 60% of primate species are threatened with extinction. Threats include deforestation, the breaking up of forests into fragments, and hunting primates for medicines, as pets and for food. Large-scale clearing of tropical forest for farming is the biggest danger. Close contact between humans and other primates can also pass on diseases, especially viruses such as herpes, measles, ebola, rabies and hepatitis.
